summaries.example: Mia looks at an empty cardboard box and imagines it is a spaceship. She is not saying the box really is a spaceship. She is pretending and thinking about a possible situation. Her picture of the spaceship may help her act out a space adventure, but it does not make the box fly.
summaries.summary: Imagination is a way of representing things without treating them as exactly real and present. We use it to think about possibilities, the past, the future, and points of view different from our own. Imagination is not the same as seeing, believing, wanting, or expecting. A person can imagine a dragon without believing that a dragon is nearby, and can imagine winning a prize without expecting to win. Philosophers study many forms of imagination. Some involve mental images, such as picturing a beach. Others involve taking an idea as part of a made-up or possible situation. Philosophers also ask whether all these activities share one basic mental power. Some theories divide imagination into types, while others try to explain many types with one general account. They discuss how imagination connects with belief, memory, pretending, art, creativity, and knowledge. There is no single answer accepted by everyone.
key_ideas: Imagination lets us think beyond what is happening right now.
Imagining is different from believing: you can imagine something without thinking it is true.
Some imaginings use mental pictures or sounds, while others are more like thinking about an idea.
Philosophers disagree about whether imagination is one single mental ability or a group of related abilities.
Imagination helps with pretend play, stories, art, creativity, understanding others, and some kinds of learning.
summaries.why_it_matters: Imagination is part of everyday thinking. It helps people play, tell stories, understand what someone else might feel, design things, and consider what could happen. It can also help with real tasks, such as deciding whether furniture will fit in a room. But imagination can go beyond reality, so we may need other ways of checking whether an imagined idea is true.

important_terms.definition: Using your mind to represent something that is not happening exactly as it is now. You can imagine the past, the future, another place, or another person’s point of view.
A picture, sound, or other sense-like experience in your mind, even when the real thing is not in front of you.
Acting as if something is true for a game or story, while knowing it is not really true in the ordinary world.
Taking something to be true. Believing and imagining can be about the same idea, but they do not work in exactly the same way.
A made-up situation or story that invites people to imagine things.

questions_to_think_about: Can you imagine something without seeing a picture in your mind?
Why does pretending that a cup is full not make the real cup full?
When might imagining help you solve a real problem?
Is remembering yesterday more like imagining or more like looking at a stored picture?

summaries.example: Suppose an engineer imagines a bridge with a different support design. The imagining may include a visual model, assumptions about forces, and a sequence of changes. It is not a belief that the bridge already exists, nor is it merely a wish that the design work. The engineer constrains the scenario using information about materials and structure. Philosophers therefore ask whether the result can provide justification for a prediction, or whether imagination only generates an idea that must later be tested.
summaries.summary: The SEP entry treats imagination as a broad and contested family of ways of representing what is not being taken as actual, present, and directly given. It can represent nonactual possibilities, past or future times, and perspectives other than the subject’s own. This basic characterization separates imagination from perception and belief, which ordinarily present their contents as actual or true, and from desire and anticipation, which involve wanting or expecting those contents. The breadth of the phenomenon creates a theoretical problem: there may be no single mental component responsible for every activity described as imaginative. One response is taxonomic. Philosophers distinguish attitude imagining from imagistic imagining, propositional from objectual contents, inside from outside perspectives, and constructive from finished episodes. Another response seeks a unified theory. Imagination has been described as simulation or recreation, a cognitive skill, a process governed by transitions between mental states, or a reducible combination of other attitudes. One radical proposal denies that imagination names a unified scientific kind, while retaining mental imagery as a useful category. Further debates concern imagination’s cognitive architecture. It may share representational structure with belief while being insulated from ordinary action and emotion through imaginative quarantining, though immersion and imaginative contagion complicate this picture. Mental imagery often resembles perception, but imagery alone may not fix what is imagined. Memory may be either a distinct kind requiring a causal connection to the past or a constructive process continuous with imagining. key_ideas: Imagination is heterogeneous: philosophical taxonomies distinguish attitude, imagistic, constructive, spontaneous, deliberate, and other forms, and these categories can overlap.
Imagination resembles belief in representational and inferential respects, but it normally does not aim at truth or guide action in the same direct way.
Mental imagery and imagination are related but not identical; an image may need a proposition, label, or broader context to determine what is being imagined.
Competing unified theories describe imagination as recreating mental states, a skill, a process of transforming other states, or not a unified kind at all.
The relationship between imagination and memory is disputed: continuists emphasize constructive similarities, while discontinuists emphasize differences such as causal links to the past.
Imagination may support creativity, engagement with art, mindreading, pretense, and knowledge, but its reliability depends on the task and the constraints placed on it.
summaries.why_it_matters: The philosophical analysis of imagination matters because it connects a familiar capacity to major questions about mind and knowledge. Imagination may help us model possibilities, understand other minds, interpret art, create new combinations, and reason through scientific thought experiments. Yet it is not automatically a reliable guide to reality: unconstrained fantasy can depart from the world, while constrained imagining may preserve or generate justification. Clarifying the varieties of imagination helps prevent one explanation from being applied too broadly and makes disagreements about memory, fiction, creativity, and cognition more precise.

important_terms.definition: A mental representation made without aiming to treat its content as actual, present, and subjectively given. It can concern possibilities, other times, or other perspectives.
Imagining that a proposition is fictional or possible, rather than using a sensory-like format such as a picture or sound.
Representing content through perception-like mental pictures, sounds, or other sensory formats.
A perception-like representation produced without the relevant external stimulus, such as picturing an object when it is absent.
A proposed common representational format for belief and attitude imagining, intended to explain why both can support similar inferences.
The idea that imagined contents are kept within a limited mental domain and normally do not guide real-world action or attitudes as beliefs do.
The view that episodic memory and imagination are distinct psychological kinds, often because genuine memory requires an appropriate causal connection to a past experience.
The view that memory and imagination are versions of a common process, distinguished partly by what they represent, such as the past, future, or merely possible events.

questions_to_think_about: If an identical mental image can represent different objects or situations, what determines its content?
Does an imagined belief-like state differ from belief because of its norm, its effects on action, or both?
Can a person with little or no conscious mental imagery still imagine? What would an answer require us to distinguish?
When do constraints make imagination a useful guide to possibility or factual knowledge?
Should a theory explain every activity called imagination, or is a useful account allowed to cover only paradigmatic cases?

summaries.example: Jordan is planning how to rearrange a bedroom. Jordan imagines the desk beside the window and mentally pictures where the chair would go. This is not the same as believing the desk is already there. Jordan also does not merely wish for a nicer room: the imagined arrangement is used to think through what would happen. If Jordan remembers the room from yesterday, that memory may also involve mental construction. Philosophers ask whether the memory and the imagined arrangement use the same kind of process, or whether remembering needs a special connection to the actual past.
summaries.summary: Imagination is a way of mentally representing something without committing to it as actually present or true. It can take us beyond the current moment: we can imagine what might happen, what happened before, or what the world looks like from someone else’s perspective. This makes imagination different from perception and belief. It also differs from desire and anticipation, because imagining something does not by itself mean wanting or expecting it. Philosophers disagree about whether imagination is one mental ability. Some build taxonomies that separate kinds of imagining. A person might imagine that a castle exists, picture the castle, imagine the castle itself, or imagine walking through it. These descriptions can overlap. Other distinctions concern whether imagining is spontaneous or deliberate, whether it fills conscious attention, and whether it is used to escape ordinary reality or to learn about it. Other philosophers seek a unified theory. They describe imagination as recreating or simulating mental states, as a skill that can be performed well and improved with practice, or as a process that changes how other mental states are organized. A different theory reduces some forms of imagination to safe thinking about possibilities, while another questions whether imagination is a single scientific category. The entry also examines imagination’s relationships with belief, mental imagery, desire, memory, supposition, and intention. Imagining can resemble believing in its reasoning patterns, yet imagined information is usually quarantined from ordinary action. This separation can weaken during pretend play, emotional responses to fiction, or immersion. Mental imagery is often part of imagination, but not all philosophers think it is required. key_ideas: The word imagination covers several activities, and philosophical categories may overlap rather than form a neat list.
Imagining and believing can make similar connections between ideas, but belief normally aims at truth and more directly guides action.
A mental image is not always enough to tell us what someone is imagining; context or a thought about the image may also matter.
Some philosophers explain imagination through simulation, skill, or mental processes; others argue that it is not one unified thing.
Memory and imagination share features such as mental construction, but philosophers disagree about whether they are fundamentally continuous.
Imagination is used in pretend play, understanding other people, art, creativity, and reasoning about what might be possible.
summaries.why_it_matters: Understanding imagination helps explain why people can enjoy fictional stories, pretend, plan, invent, and consider other people’s thoughts without confusing these activities with ordinary belief. It also shows why imagination can be both useful and risky. A carefully constrained imagined scene may help with planning or learning, while an unconstrained one may have little connection to how things really are. Studying the differences among imagining, remembering, supposing, and believing gives us better tools for thinking about our own minds.

important_terms.definition: Representing something without treating it as how things actually are, here and now. It can concern possibilities, other times, or another person’s viewpoint.
Imagining that a statement is part of a fictional or possible situation, without accepting it as true.
Imagining by using a picture-like, sound-like, or other sense-like representation in the mind.
A mind-made representation that resembles perception even though the matching object or event is not currently stimulating the senses.
A mental activity of considering a hypothetical statement and working out what would follow from it.
The normal separation between imagined events and the real world, so imagined events usually do not directly change real beliefs or actions.
The view that memory and imagination are different kinds of mental process, often because memory requires a suitable link to a past experience.
The view that remembering and imagining use the same general kind of constructive process, with differences in what each is directed toward.

questions_to_think_about: Why might someone imagine a scary monster but not believe one is in the room?
Could two people have the same mental picture but imagine different things?
What might make a memory different from an imagined event?
Does imagining a possible invention help prove that it could really work?
Can imagination affect real behavior even if imagined events are normally kept separate from reality?
